items.prompt: What is a 'deployment,' as this unit defines it?
choices: The process of taking a new version of code from a built artifact to a running, live traffic-serving service
Any commit pushed to the main branch
The act of writing a new feature
A backup of the production database
items.explanation: Deployment specifically refers to getting new code live and serving traffic — writing the code or committing it are separate, earlier steps.
items.reference:
Deployment
built artifact → running, live service

Why: Distinguishing deployment from earlier steps (writing, committing code) matters because this unit is specifically about what happens at the moment new code goes live.

items.prompt: In the opening scenario, at which point does the 'deployment' actually happen?
choices: When the engineer SSHes in and runs the pull/install/restart sequence to bring the new version live
When the new dependency is first added to the codebase
When the engineer writes the code for the new feature
When the pull request is opened for review
items.explanation: The deployment is the act of bringing the new code live on the running service — everything before that (writing, adding a dependency, opening a PR) is preparation, not deployment itself.
items.reference:
Deployment
built artifact → running, live service

Why: Distinguishing deployment from earlier steps (writing, committing code) matters because this unit is specifically about what happens at the moment new code goes live.

items.prompt: What does 'idempotency' mean in the context of a deploy?
choices: Running the same deploy steps twice, or replaying them after a partial failure, produces the same correct end state rather than compounding errors
The deploy runs faster every time it's repeated
Every deploy must use a completely different set of steps
The deploy can only ever be run exactly once, ever
items.explanation: Idempotency is specifically about safety under repetition or partial failure — replaying the same steps shouldn't leave the system in a worse or inconsistent state.
items.reference:
Idempotency
same steps, run twice → same correct end state

Why: A deploy that fails partway through needs to be safely re-runnable, not something that compounds the damage on a second attempt.

items.prompt: Why does idempotency matter specifically when a deploy fails partway through?
choices: Because re-running the same steps should safely reach the correct end state, instead of requiring a human to figure out exactly what already happened
Because it makes the deploy run in half the time
Because it prevents the deploy from ever failing in the first place
It only matters for deploys that touch a database
items.explanation: A partial failure is exactly the scenario idempotency protects against — being able to safely re-run the same steps means nobody has to manually reconstruct what state the system was left in.
items.reference:
Idempotency
same steps, run twice → same correct end state

Why: A deploy that fails partway through needs to be safely re-runnable, not something that compounds the damage on a second attempt.

items.prompt: What is 'repeatability,' as this unit defines it?
choices: The exact same sequence of steps runs the same way every time, regardless of who triggers the deploy
The ability to deploy multiple times per day
Running the same code on multiple servers at once
A deploy that never needs to be repeated
items.explanation: Repeatability is about consistency across who runs it and when — this is exactly what a manual checklist can't guarantee, since it depends on the person following it correctly.
items.reference:
Repeatability
same steps, same order, every time — regardless of who runs it

Why: A checklist followed by a human is only as repeatable as that human's memory and attention on a given day.

items.prompt: In the opening scenario, what specifically broke repeatability on Deploy 9?
choices: A different, rushed engineer ran the same nominal steps but skipped one of them
The server hardware was different on Deploy 9
The deploy was run at a different time of day than usual
Repeatability was never broken — the outage was unrelated to the deploy process
items.explanation: The steps were nominally the same, but a human executing them from memory under time pressure didn't actually run all of them — that gap between 'nominally the same process' and 'actually the same steps every time' is what repeatability is about.
items.reference:
Repeatability
same steps, same order, every time — regardless of who runs it

Why: A checklist followed by a human is only as repeatable as that human's memory and attention on a given day.

items.prompt: What is an 'atomic switch,' as this unit defines it?
choices: Flipping traffic from the old version to the new one in a single, instantaneous step, so no request ever hits a half-updated state
Restarting the service as fast as possible
Switching to a different server during high traffic
Any change made without informing the team first
items.explanation: Atomic specifically means there's no in-between state a request could observe — the switch either hasn't happened yet, or it's fully complete.
items.reference:
Atomic switch
old version ↔ new version
no window where a request sees a mix of both

Why: Without atomicity, a request could observe files from two different releases at once.

items.prompt: Why is a symlink swap a good example of an atomic switch?
choices: The pointer either references the old release directory or the new one — never something in between
Symlinks are always faster than copying files
Symlinks automatically run health checks
Symlinks prevent the need for a rollback entirely
items.explanation: A symlink's target is a single value that changes in one step — there's no partial state where it points at both directories at once, which is exactly the atomicity property this unit cares about.
items.reference:
Atomic switch
old version ↔ new version
no window where a request sees a mix of both

Why: Without atomicity, a request could observe files from two different releases at once.

items.prompt: What is 'rollback,' as this unit defines it?
choices: Automatically reverting to the last known-good version when a new deploy fails a health check
Manually re-typing the previous version's code from memory
Deleting the failed deploy's logs so it looks like nothing happened
Waiting until the next scheduled deploy to fix a broken release
items.explanation: Rollback specifically means the reversion happens automatically, triggered by the health check's result — not that someone has to notice and manually intervene.
items.reference:
Rollback
health check fails → automatically revert to last known-good version

Why: An automatic rollback removes the need for anyone to notice a problem before recovery starts.

items.prompt: What would have actually prevented the Deploy 9 outage, according to this unit?
choices: A health check running before traffic switched, wired to an automatic rollback — not a stricter checklist
Requiring two engineers to be present for every deploy
Deploying only once a month instead of more frequently
Writing more detailed comments in the wiki page's checklist
items.explanation: A stricter checklist still depends on a human following it correctly — an automatic health check and rollback removes that dependency entirely.
items.reference:
Rollback
health check fails → automatically revert to last known-good version

Why: An automatic rollback removes the need for anyone to notice a problem before recovery starts.

items.prompt: According to this unit, what's the real difference between a wiki-page checklist and a scripted deploy?
choices: A checklist documents the steps but doesn't enforce that they all happen; a script executes the same fixed sequence every time
A checklist is always shorter than a script
A script requires more people to run it than a checklist
There's no real difference — both are equally reliable
items.explanation: The gap between documentation and enforcement is exactly the failure mode from Deploy 9 — the checklist existed, it just wasn't followed exactly.
items.reference:
Checklist vs. script
checklist: documents steps
script: enforces steps

Why: Documentation and enforcement are not the same thing — this distinction is the core of the whole unit.

items.prompt: Why did eight successful manual deploys not prove the process was safe?
choices: A manual process's safety depends on the person running it, and that dependency can fail on any given attempt, not just statistically rare ones
Eight deploys is too few to ever prove anything about any process
The eight successful deploys were actually scripted, not manual
The server itself became less reliable over time
items.explanation: Past successes don't establish that the process itself is safe — they only show that, so far, whoever ran it happened to remember every step correctly.
items.reference:
Checklist vs. script
checklist: documents steps
script: enforces steps

Why: Documentation and enforcement are not the same thing — this distinction is the core of the whole unit.

items.prompt: The opening scenario asks what changed between Deploy 8 and Deploy 9. What's the actual answer?
choices: Nothing about the steps changed — a different, rushed person ran the same nominal process and skipped one of them
The server's hardware was upgraded between the two deploys
Deploy 9 used a completely different set of steps than Deploy 8
A new testing framework was introduced right before Deploy 9
items.explanation: The steps themselves were unchanged — what changed was who ran them and under what conditions, which is exactly the variable a manual checklist can't control for.
items.reference:
What changed between Deploy 8 and 9
steps: unchanged
person running them: different, rushed

Why: If the steps themselves are the same but the outcome differs, the process — not the steps — is where the fix has to happen.

items.prompt: Why does the opening scenario emphasize that a *different* engineer ran Deploy 9, in a hurry?
choices: To show that the process's safety depended on a specific person's careful memory, not on anything the process itself guaranteed
To suggest that only that specific engineer should be blamed for the outage
Because only certain engineers are allowed to run deploys
It's an irrelevant detail included only for narrative color
items.explanation: The detail matters precisely because it shows the checklist's correctness was riding on a specific person's attention that day, not on any guarantee built into the process.
items.reference:
What changed between Deploy 8 and 9
steps: unchanged
person running them: different, rushed

Why: If the steps themselves are the same but the outcome differs, the process — not the steps — is where the fix has to happen.

items.prompt: According to L2's pipeline diagram, why does the health check run before the atomic symlink switch, not after?
choices: Checking health before the switch decides whether traffic should ever reach the new release; checking after would mean users already hit the broken version
It's purely a stylistic convention with no functional impact
Health checks are only meaningful once traffic is already flowing
The order doesn't actually matter as long as both steps eventually run
items.explanation: The whole point of the health check is to gate traffic — running it after the switch would defeat that purpose, since users would already be affected by the time the check ran.
items.reference:
Pipeline order
extract → install → migrate → health check → switch → restart

Why: The switch is deliberately the last thing that can go wrong — everything before it happens against a release that isn't live yet.

items.prompt: Why do extraction, dependency install, and migrations all happen before the health check, while the old release stays live?
choices: So that preparing the new release can't affect users at all — the old release keeps serving every request until the switch actually happens
Because those steps are always the slowest and must run first for performance reasons
Because migrations must always run after the health check, never before
It's an arbitrary ordering with no bearing on safety
items.explanation: Doing all the preparation work in the new release directory while the old one stays live means nothing about preparing the new version can disrupt current traffic — only the final switch can.
items.reference:
Pipeline order
extract → install → migrate → health check → switch → restart

Why: The switch is deliberately the last thing that can go wrong — everything before it happens against a release that isn't live yet.

items.prompt: According to L2, what specifically goes wrong if a deploy overwrites the old release's files in place instead of switching a symlink?
choices: There's a window where some files on disk belong to the old version and some to the new one, and a request could read a mix of both
In-place overwrites are always slower than a symlink switch
Nothing goes wrong — the two approaches are functionally identical
In-place overwrites make rollback completely impossible
items.explanation: Overwriting files one at a time creates a period where the release is neither fully old nor fully new — a symlink switch has no equivalent window because the pointer only ever has one value at a time.
items.reference:
Why atomicity matters
in-place overwrite: mixed-version window possible
symlink switch: no such window

Why: A request that reads a mix of old and new files can behave in ways neither version was ever tested for.

items.prompt: Why does a symlink pointer specifically avoid the mixed-version window that in-place file overwrites create?
choices: The pointer's target is a single value that changes in one step — it either references the old directory or the new one, never both at once
Symlinks are stored in a special part of the disk that updates instantly across all files
Symlinks automatically pause incoming requests during the switch
They don't actually avoid it — symlinks have the same window as in-place overwrites
items.explanation: Because the symlink's target is a single atomic value rather than many individual files being changed one at a time, there's no intermediate state to observe.
items.reference:
Why atomicity matters
in-place overwrite: mixed-version window possible
symlink switch: no such window

Why: A request that reads a mix of old and new files can behave in ways neither version was ever tested for.

items.prompt: According to L2's comparison table, how is a skipped step handled differently between a manual checklist and a scripted pipeline?
choices: A manual checklist can silently skip a step and the omission may be invisible until it fails; a scripted pipeline has no path that skips a step
Both handle skipped steps identically — neither can prevent one
A scripted pipeline can skip steps just as easily as a manual checklist, just faster
Manual checklists are actually more reliable at catching skipped steps
items.explanation: The core difference is reachability — a script's unconditional steps aren't a 'usually happens' outcome, they're the only outcome the function can produce.
items.reference:
Manual vs. scripted
Skipped stepmanual: possible, often invisible / scripted: not reachable
Bad deploy recoverymanual: someone notices, re-runs steps / scripted: automatic rollback

Why: This is exactly the gap that let Deploy 9's missed step go unnoticed until the restart crashed.

items.prompt: According to L2's comparison table, how does recovering from a bad deploy differ between manual and scripted approaches?
choices: Manually, someone has to notice the problem and re-run the old steps by hand; scripted, the rollback step runs automatically on health-check failure
Recovery is identical in both cases — a human always has to intervene either way
A scripted pipeline can never recover automatically, only a human can trigger a rollback
Manual recovery is always faster because a human can react instantly
items.explanation: The scripted pipeline's rollback is conditioned directly on the health check's own result, with no human-notices-then-acts step in between.
items.reference:
Manual vs. scripted
Skipped stepmanual: possible, often invisible / scripted: not reachable
Bad deploy recoverymanual: someone notices, re-runs steps / scripted: automatic rollback

Why: This is exactly the gap that let Deploy 9's missed step go unnoticed until the restart crashed.

items.prompt: According to L2's generalizable lesson, is this unit really only about `npm install` and deploy scripts specifically?
choices: No — it applies to any multi-step operational process where a human is trusted to remember and correctly sequence steps under time pressure
Yes, the lesson only applies to Node.js dependency installation
No, but it only applies to processes involving symlinks
Yes, this lesson is specific to deploys and doesn't generalize
items.explanation: The `npm install` detail is one instance of a broader pattern: any process depending on a human doing the right thing in the right order will eventually fail that trust.
items.reference:
The general lesson
fewer steps depending on human memory → fewer ways a normal day becomes an incident

Why: Recognizing the general pattern is what lets you spot the same risk in processes that have nothing to do with deploys.

items.prompt: Why does this unit say people being careless isn't the real explanation for incidents like Deploy 9?
choices: Human memory under time pressure isn't a reliable substitute for a machine that executes the same steps the same way regardless of how the day is going
Because the engineer on Deploy 9 was specifically known to be careless in general
Because carelessness is impossible to prevent, so it isn't worth discussing
Because the real cause was always a hardware failure, not a process failure
items.explanation: The point isn't that anyone was careless — it's that relying on memory under pressure is structurally unreliable regardless of who's doing it, which is why the fix is process-level, not person-level.
items.reference:
The general lesson
fewer steps depending on human memory → fewer ways a normal day becomes an incident

Why: Recognizing the general pattern is what lets you spot the same risk in processes that have nothing to do with deploys.

items.prompt: Why does the pipeline extract the new release into its own directory, rather than modifying the currently-live release's files directly?
choices: So that preparing the new version can't affect currently-served traffic — the live release stays fully untouched until the switch
Because extracting into a new directory is required by the operating system
It's purely to save disk space compared to overwriting in place
So that the new release can be extracted more quickly than the old one was
items.explanation: Keeping the new release entirely separate from the live one until the switch means every preparation step is risk-free with respect to current traffic — there's no way extraction or installation can degrade what users are seeing right now.
items.reference:
Separate directories
old release directory: live, untouched
new release directory: being prepared, not yet serving traffic

Why: Only the switch step can affect live traffic — everything before it is reversible with zero user impact.

items.prompt: If dependency installation fails partway through, why is that failure harmless to current users under this pipeline design?
choices: The failure only affects the new release's not-yet-live directory — the old release keeps serving every request unaffected
The pipeline automatically pauses all incoming traffic during dependency installation
Dependency installation failures are always silently ignored by design
It isn't harmless — any failed step immediately takes the service offline
items.explanation: Because installation happens in the new release's own directory, a failure there simply means the new release never becomes ready to switch to — the currently-live old release is completely unaffected.
items.reference:
Separate directories
old release directory: live, untouched
new release directory: being prepared, not yet serving traffic

Why: Only the switch step can affect live traffic — everything before it is reversible with zero user impact.

items.prompt: Why do migrations run before the atomic switch rather than after it?
choices: The new code shouldn't go live until the database schema it depends on is already in place — running migrations after the switch would mean new code briefly runs against an old schema
Migrations are always faster to run before a restart than after one
It's an arbitrary convention with no functional consequence
Because the health check requires migrations to already be reflected in its output
items.explanation: If the switch happened first, the new code would start receiving traffic and querying a database schema that hasn't been updated yet — running migrations first avoids that mismatch entirely.
items.reference:
Migration order
migrations run against the not-yet-live new release
switch only happens once schema + code are both ready

Why: New code and the schema it expects need to arrive together — splitting them across the switch creates a window of mismatch.

items.prompt: What would go wrong if the pipeline switched traffic to the new release before its required migrations had run?
choices: The new code would briefly run against a database schema it wasn't written for, since the schema change hasn't happened yet
Nothing — migrations and code deploys are always independent of each other
The switch itself would automatically fail and roll back on its own
The old release would be deleted before the new one was ready
items.explanation: Code and the schema it depends on need to change together — switching traffic before the schema catches up means the new code is querying a database it wasn't written against.
items.reference:
Migration order
migrations run against the not-yet-live new release
switch only happens once schema + code are both ready

Why: New code and the schema it expects need to arrive together — splitting them across the switch creates a window of mismatch.

items.prompt: In the pipeline diagram, what specifically triggers the rollback branch?
choices: The health check step returning an unhealthy result
A human clicking a 'rollback' button after noticing something is wrong
A fixed timer that always rolls back exactly ten minutes after every deploy
The restart-service step being skipped
items.explanation: The rollback branch is wired directly to the health check's outcome — there's no human-in-the-loop step between 'something's wrong' and 'roll back.'
items.reference:
What triggers rollback
health check unhealthy → rollback branch
health check healthy → switch branch

Why: The trigger being mechanical rather than human-observed is what makes the rollback reliably fast.

items.prompt: Why does wiring rollback directly to the health check's result matter more than just having a rollback procedure documented somewhere?
choices: A documented procedure still requires a human to notice the problem and remember to run it; a wired trigger requires neither
Documentation is actually more reliable than any automated trigger
It doesn't matter — both approaches produce identical recovery times in practice
Wiring it directly makes the rollback permanent and unable to be reverted later
items.explanation: A documented rollback procedure has the same weakness as the original checklist — it depends on a human noticing and acting. Wiring it to the health check removes that dependency.
items.reference:
What triggers rollback
health check unhealthy → rollback branch
health check healthy → switch branch

Why: The trigger being mechanical rather than human-observed is what makes the rollback reliably fast.

items.prompt: According to L3's 'extend it' section, why might a health check need to retry a few times instead of failing on the very first check?
choices: A freshly-restarted, perfectly healthy service can take a moment to warm up, so an immediate first check might fail even though nothing is actually wrong
Retries are required by convention and have no functional purpose
A single health check is always 100% accurate, so retries only add unnecessary delay
Retrying makes the rollback happen faster when a deploy is genuinely broken
items.explanation: Treating a slow warm-up the same as a genuine failure would trigger unnecessary rollbacks on perfectly good deploys — retries give a healthy-but-slow-starting service a fair chance to pass.
items.reference:
Retry trade-off
too few retries → healthy deploys rolled back unnecessarily
too many retries → broken deploys stay live longer

Why: Every retry policy is a trade-off between false rollbacks and slow detection — there's no retry count that eliminates both risks.

items.prompt: What's the trade-off in choosing how many retry attempts a health check gets before giving up?

There's no real trade-off — more retries are always strictly better with no downside
Fewer retries always mean a faster, more accurate health check
The number of retries has no effect on rollback timing at all
items.explanation: This is a genuine two-sided trade-off: the retry count has to balance not punishing healthy deploys against not leaving a broken deploy live for too long.
items.reference:
Retry trade-off
too few retries → healthy deploys rolled back unnecessarily
too many retries → broken deploys stay live longer

The failure modes table doesn't address this — it only covers atomic switches

items.prompt: L3 says changing what `buildDeploySteps` returns requires 'a deliberate, reviewable edit.' Why does that distinction matter compared to a manual mistake?
choices: A code change goes through review before it can affect any deploy, while a manual mistake happens in the moment with no equivalent check

Because code changes are always automatically tested before merging, with no exceptions
Because manual mistakes are actually easier to review than code changes

Deliberate edit vs. in-the-moment mistake
code change: reviewable before it takes effect
manual mistake: takes effect immediately, unreviewed

items.prompt: If someone genuinely needed to change the deploy pipeline's steps, how would that happen under the scripted approach versus the manual one?
choices: Under the scripted approach, it requires editing and reviewing the function's code; under the manual approach, it could happen silently as an in-the-moment slip
Both approaches require the exact same level of review and visibility
The manual approach actually makes changes more visible, since a human explicitly performs each step
Neither approach allows the steps to ever be changed once established
items.explanation: The scripted approach forces any real change through code review; the manual approach has no such barrier, which is exactly why an unintended change (a skipped step) could happen without anyone deciding it should.
